title: Scaffolds easier to read than the text
statement: Write instructions, prompts, feedback and anything a lesson's guide says at an easier reading level than the text they support, and keep internal design terms out of them.
example: One course's checklist keeps every passage within 420 to 650 on a reading-level scale and every instruction below that band.
detail: The walkthrough of a built Grade 3 lesson sets child-facing prose at 420–650L, below the passage, warm and without jargon, because the scaffold must be easier to read than the thing it scaffolds (`downloads/SUPERSEDED — see v2.1_ WITW Lesson 1 learning walkthrough v2 (table format).md`, line 38). The internal name of the procedure the lesson teaches never reaches the child; its introduction speaks in what-we-will-do terms instead (`downloads/SUPERSEDED — see v2 (table format)_ WITW Lesson 1 learning walkthrough.md`, line 181). A checklist for the same lessons gives 420–650L as the passage band and puts instructional lines below it (`grade3-reading/artifacts/AlphaRead-QC-Checklist-v2-2026-09-04.md`, line 64).
against: The script the row cites as its verifier was not found, so until it is the row runs as an agent's reading (`grade3-reading/artifacts/AlphaRead-QC-Checklist-v2-2026-09-04.md`).

What a viewer reads at a film's stops (the questions, options and feedback) speaks of the film, never of how it is … made: no beat, cue, caption or frame.
an untrue feedback line, "the second frame", and wrong-option feedback that named the answer: new checks, below;
code: no "beat", "cue", "caption" or "frame", and no wrong-option feedback that names the answer;
what a viewer reads at a stop: no making words, and a wrong option's feedback does not name the answer
Note that NN/g's "write at a 6th-grade level" advice is for interface copy, *not* for the grade 9 passages.
Interface copy is instruction. Internal organizer names are not neutral when a child must decode them before acting.
Step names ("Retrieval") are our jargon, not the student's
